read: full: pp.1-22 (abstract, introduction, related work, scope, taxonomy and difficulty rubric, construction, evaluation protocol, benchmarking study, circularity argument, limitations, release) read in full; reference list pp.22-26 skimmed, EngTrace entry [29] checked (p.25). Figures 1-5 are images with no text layer.
venue_now: Not shown in the text: page 1 carries no journal header and no arXiv stamp (MANIFEST.json: fetched from arxiv.org/pdf/2603.02239). The catalogue's 'Computers & Industrial Engineering 2026' cannot be confirmed from this file.
what_it_is: ERI is a taxonomy-driven instruction dataset for training and evaluating engineering LLMs: nine fields and 55 subdomains crossed with seven intent types (definition, explanation, calculation, comparison, design, troubleshooting, code) and three tiers (undergraduate, graduate, professional), 50 instruction-response pairs per cell, 57,750 records in all (pp.1, 5-9). Both the questions and the reference responses were generated by an LLM (GPT-5 Mini) from seed tuples and then filtered by schema checks, deduplication and length; a GPT-5.1 quality rating of a random 10% sample is described but its results are not reported (pp.9-12, 18). In the benchmarking study seven models answered a stratified 10% subset (over 5,000 items) and three LLM judges from different providers scored each response 1-5 against the generated reference, averaged (pp.13-14). No human checked the items, the references or the judges; the paper substitutes a 'convergent validity' argument from agreement among the evaluated models (p.18).
domain: engineering: civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, environmental, aerospace, materials and industrial engineering and fire science (nine fields, 55 subdomains; Table 1, p.6); seven intent types including calculation, design, troubleshooting and code
size: 57,750 generated records (1,155 cells x 50; pp.1, 5); the released splits hold 45,415 train, 2,671 validation and 5,343 test rows, 53,429 in all (p.22); seven models evaluated on a stratified 10% subset of over 5,000 items (p.13); 115,962 judgments (p.14)
source_of_items: generated by an LLM (GPT-5 Mini) from (field, subdomain, intent, difficulty) seed tuples, five pairs per API call and ten calls per tuple; the reference answers are the generator's own responses (pp.9-10, 18)
instances: static (generated once by an LLM and released as fixed JSONL splits, p.22)
has_gold_traces: partial: every record has an LLM-generated reference response, and for calculation items the success criterion asks for key steps and a final answer with units (Table 2, p.7); these references are unverified and are not used for any step-level check
evaluation: LLM judge: three judges (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Mistral Small 3) each score a response 1-5 against the reference answer and the mean is reported (p.14); the harness also flags empty outputs, refusals, missing final answers and violations of parsable numeric bounds (pp.12-13). The per-dimension rubric of Table 3 (accuracy, units, method, assumptions, verification, clarity, realism, traceability; pp.8-9) is described, but the study reports only the single holistic 1-5 score.
human_validation: None reported. A GPT-5.1 model rates a random 10% of records on a five-point quality scale, with no results given (p.12). The 'convergent validation' is model-based: the three frontier models each scored 4.0 or above on 68.8% of items and 3.0 or below on 1.7% (read by the authors as a bound on hallucinated references), and smaller models beat frontier models on under 0.1% of items (p.18). The paper names 'the absence of human-verified ground truth' as a concern and defers expert validation of a stratified subsample to future work (pp.18, 20). Only inter-judge agreement is measured: Spearman 0.70-0.80, over 85% within one point (p.14).
contamination_measures: none: the records are public (Hugging Face, GitHub) with fixed train/validation/test splits (pp.1, 22); exact and optional semantic deduplication target redundancy, not contamination (p.12)

engtrace_use.explanation: Not cited in the May paper. Paragraph: engineering, beside or in place of the generalist-suite sentence (May p.2: MMLU, BIG-Bench and SuperGPQA 'restrict assessment to factual recall via multiple-choice questions'). ERI is the largest multi-field engineering benchmark among the candidates and its nine fields include all five EngTrace branches (Table 1, p.6), so a reviewer would expect it; it is open-ended, not multiple-choice, so it cannot be folded into the May MCQ sentence. The contrast EngTrace must state: ERI's questions and reference answers are generated by an LLM and never verified by people (pp.18, 20); its scores are holistic 1-5 LLM-judge ratings against those references (p.14); and its judges share providers with the models they rank (OpenAI: GPT-5 Mini generates, GPT-5 is evaluated, GPT-4.1 Mini judges; Anthropic: Claude Sonnet 4 is evaluated, Claude Haiku 4.5 judges; Mistral: Mistral 7B is evaluated, Mistral Small 3 judges; pp.14, 17, 18). EngTrace's answers and milestones are computed by template code and checked deterministically, its residual judge comes from outside the roster and was validated against experts, and its pool is drawn from a private seed.

suggested_wording: ERI (Naser et al., 2026) spans nine engineering fields with 57,750 instruction-response records, but both its questions and its reference answers are generated by an LLM, and responses are scored holistically by a panel of LLM judges against those references, with no human verification of either.
facts_to_cite: Nine engineering fields (civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, environmental, aerospace, materials, fire, industrial) and 55 subdomains, crossed with seven intent types and three difficulty tiers (undergraduate, graduate, professional), for 57,750 records (p.1; Table 1, p.6).
Each field-subdomain-intent-difficulty cell holds 50 instruction-response pairs, 1,155 cells in all (p.5).
Questions and reference responses are generated by GPT-5 Mini, five pairs per API call and ten calls per seed tuple, as strict JSON (pp.9-10, 18).

Post-processing: schema validation, exact deduplication on lowercased instructions, optional embedding-based deduplication, length filtering, and a GPT-5.1 five-point quality rating of a random 10% sample (p.12).

Seven models were evaluated on a stratified 10% subset of over 5,000 items (p.13); three LLM judges (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Mistral Small 3) scored each response 1-5 against the reference answer and the scores were averaged, 115,962 judgments in all (p.14).
Inter-judge Spearman correlations ranged from 0.70 to 0.80, with over 85% of judge pairs within one point (p.14).
Mean scores: GPT-5 4.48, Claude Sonnet 4 4.31, DeepSeek V3.1 4.30 (p.14); Mistral 7B 3.81, Llama 3.3 70B 3.75, Qwen 2.5 7B 3.27, Llama 3.1 8B 2.96 (p.17).
Scores fall from undergraduate to professional to graduate items; GPT-5 loses 0.06 points (1.4%) from undergraduate to graduate, the 7-8B models 0.30-0.32 (pp.17-18).

The paper acknowledges 'the absence of human-verified ground truth' and argues from model agreement instead; frontier models scored 3.0 or below on 1.7% of items, which it reads as a bound on hallucinated references (p.18); expert validation of a subsample is future work (pp.18, 20).
The released dataset has 45,415 train, 2,671 validation and 5,343 test rows (p.22).
ERI cites EngTrace's arXiv version as an 'entirely synthetic' dataset (p.9; reference [29], p.25).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-branch engineering scope (its nine fields include civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical and industrial; Table 1, p.6), three difficulty tiers (pp.7-8), synthetic construction and a calculation intent. Lacks: answers computed by code (the references are GPT-5 Mini outputs, p.18); gold intermediate values or traces usable for checking; step-level evaluation (one holistic 1-5 judge score, p.14); any human validation of items, references or judges (pp.18, 20); contamination control (public fixed splits, p.22); judge independence (judge providers overlap the evaluated models, pp.14, 17). Beyond ERI, EngTrace should claim: code-derived gold answers and milestones, deterministic answer, milestone and arithmetic checks, a residual judge from outside the roster validated against 15 experts, and items drawn from a private seed.
notes: Paragraph: engineering. (1) Do not repeat the search note's 'cross-provider' reading of ERI's validation: the claim that generator, evaluated models and judges 'share no training pipeline' (p.18) is undercut by the paper's own model lists (pp.14, 17), and it says the seven evaluated models come from 'four providers' (p.18) when they come from six. (2) The 1.7% is the share of items on which frontier models scored 3.0 or below, read by the authors as a hallucination bound (p.18); it is not a measured error rate and should not be cited as one. (3) ERI quotes EngTrace's phrase 'entirely synthetic' (p.9) as support for LLM-generated data; in the May paper that phrase opens a limitation (May p.9), and EngTrace's synthetic items are computed by template code, not generated by an LLM; the revision may want to draw that distinction. (4) Internal inconsistencies: 57,750 generated records against 53,429 released rows (p.22); the Conclusions call it 'Engineering Reasoning and Intelligence' (p.21); 'Data is available on request from the author' (p.22) sits beside the public links. (5) Graduate items, not professional ones, score lowest (p.17).
